title: Moles, Stoichiometry and Gases
bigQuestion: How can chemists count atoms they cannot see, and predict exactly how much gas a reaction will make?

story.title: Thirty Milliseconds
story.kicker: A crash sensor fires, a solid turns to gas, and a bag fills before your head can move.
paragraphs: A car on the Eisenhower Expressway slows for traffic. The car behind it does not. At the moment of impact, a tiny sensor bolted to the frame feels the sudden deceleration and closes an electrical switch. Current flows into an igniter no bigger than a pencil eraser. The whole event, from impact to a fully inflated airbag, takes about 30 milliseconds. A human eye blink takes longer.

Inside the steering wheel sits a metal canister holding a few dozen grams of a white powder. For decades the powder was sodium azide, NaN3. It is a solid, dense and quiet, until the igniter heats it past roughly 300 degrees Celsius. Then every sodium azide unit breaks apart into sodium metal and nitrogen gas. The equation is short: 2 NaN3 gives 2 Na plus 3 N2. The nitrogen is the point. Three molecules of gas appear for every two units of solid.

That is a lot of gas. One mole of any gas at room temperature fills about 24 liters, roughly the volume of a large backpack. Sixty grams of sodium azide is about 0.9 mole of the solid, which becomes about 1.4 moles of nitrogen, which fills about 34 liters. The bag is designed to hold just that much. Engineers did not guess. They counted atoms by weighing, then used the ratio in the balanced equation to fix the mass of powder to the size of the bag.

Sodium metal is dangerous on its own. It reacts violently with water, including the water in a person's eyes and lungs. So the canister also holds potassium nitrate and silica. The hot sodium reacts with the nitrate, releasing a little more nitrogen, and the leftover metal oxides melt into the silica to form a harmless glassy solid. What reaches the driver is warm nitrogen, the same gas that makes up 78 percent of every breath.

The airbag is chemistry on a stopwatch. It depends on a solid that stays stable for fifteen years in a hot parked car, then decomposes completely in a few thousandths of a second. It depends on knowing the exact number of gas molecules a given mass of powder will produce. Every idea in this chapter, the mole, the balanced equation, the limiting reactant and the gas laws, was worked out long before anyone imagined a car, and every one of them is at work in that white bag.
story.think: The bag must inflate fully but not burst. What two quantities would an engineer need to know before choosing how many grams of powder to put in the canister?

lessons.title: The Mole
lessons.mainIdea: A mole is a fixed, enormous number of particles, chosen so that the mass of one mole in grams equals the atomic mass on the periodic table.
reading: Pour a teaspoon of water into your palm. It holds about 5 grams. It also holds about 170,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 molecules. No balance can count them, and no one would want to. Chemists needed a way to talk about huge numbers of tiny particles the way a baker talks about a dozen eggs. The answer was a counting unit called the *mole*.

One mole is 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd power particles. That number is *Avogadro's number*, named for the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, though he never knew its value. The number is not random. It was chosen so that one mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass of exactly 12 grams, matching the atomic mass on the periodic table. Since 2019, the mole has been defined as exactly 6.02214076 times 10 to the 23rd power particles, so the link to carbon is now a very close approximation rather than a definition.

The payoff is simple. The periodic table lists the mass of one atom in atomic mass units. Read that same number in grams, and you have the mass of one mole of atoms. One iron atom has a mass of about 55.8 atomic mass units. One mole of iron, a small cube you could hold, has a mass of about 55.8 grams. Weigh 55.8 grams of iron, and you have counted out 602,200,000,000,000,000,000,000 atoms without seeing a single one.

How big is a mole? A mole of pennies, spread across the whole surface of Earth, would make a layer hundreds of kilometers deep. A mole of grains of sand would cover the entire United States far deeper than any building. Yet a mole of water molecules is only about 18 milliliters, a few sips. Atoms are small enough that a number this absurd is exactly the right size for a glass of water.

words.d: the chemist's counting unit: 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd power particles of anything
the number of particles in one mole, about 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd power
a unit of mass equal to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, used for single atoms
the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole

look.title: Avogadro's Bold Guess, 1811
look.text: Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of any gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules. He argued this could explain why gases combine in simple whole-number volume ratios, as Gay-Lussac had measured. Most chemists ignored the idea for nearly fifty years.
look.cite: Amedeo Avogadro, essay in the Journal de Physique, 1811 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: If equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, what could you learn by weighing one liter of hydrogen and one liter of oxygen?

check.q: What is the mass of one mole of carbon-12 atoms?
check.why: The mole was chosen so that one mole of carbon-12 has a mass of 12 grams, matching its atomic mass.

check.q: A student says a mole is a unit of mass. What is wrong with that?
choices: Nothing; a mole always equals 12 grams
A mole is a number of particles, and its mass depends on what the particles are
A mole is a unit of volume, not mass
A mole only applies to gases
check.why: A mole is a count, like a dozen. A mole of iron and a mole of water have different masses because the particles differ.

check.q: Which sample contains the most atoms?
check.why: Number of atoms depends only on moles, not on the element. Two moles is twice as many atoms as one, no matter how heavy each atom is.

lessons.title: Molar Mass of a Compound
lessons.mainIdea: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula, and it tells you what fraction of the mass each element supplies.
reading: Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom per molecule. To find the mass of a mole of water, add up the atoms. Hydrogen is 1.008 grams per mole, and there are two, so 2.016 grams. Oxygen is 15.999 grams per mole. The total is about 18.02 grams per mole. That is why a mole of water is such a small puddle: 18 grams is about a tablespoon and a bit.

The same addition works for anything with a formula. Table salt, NaCl, is 22.99 plus 35.45, about 58.44 grams per mole. Carbon dioxide, CO2, is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, about 44.01 grams per mole. Glucose, C6H12O6, is six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens, about 180.16 grams per mole. Be careful with subscripts and parentheses. Calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, has two nitrate groups, so two nitrogens and six oxygens.

Once you know a molar mass, you can find the *percent composition*: what share of the mass belongs to each element. In water, hydrogen supplies 2.016 grams of every 18.02, about 11 percent, and oxygen supplies the other 89 percent. That number surprises people. Water is mostly hydrogen by count of atoms but mostly oxygen by mass, because each oxygen atom is about sixteen times heavier than each hydrogen.

Percent composition is how chemists check what they have made. If a lab produces a white powder and claims it is pure sodium chloride, the powder should be 39.3 percent sodium by mass. Burn a sample of a new compound, capture the carbon dioxide and water, weigh them, and you can work backwards to the ratio of atoms in the original. That is how the formulas of thousands of natural substances, from caffeine to vitamin C, were first worked out.

words.d: the percentage of a compound's mass that each element contributes
the symbols and subscripts that state how many atoms of each element are in one unit of a compound
the small number after a symbol that tells how many of that atom are in the formula

look.title: Molar Masses of Common Elements
look.prompt: Use the table to find the molar mass of sodium azide, NaN3. Then explain why nitrogen makes up most of its mass.

check.q: What is the approximate molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO2?
check.why: One carbon (12.01) plus two oxygens (2 times 16.00) gives about 44 g/mol.

check.q: Water is mostly oxygen by mass even though it has twice as many hydrogen atoms. Why?
choices: Oxygen atoms are much heavier than hydrogen atoms
There are actually more oxygen atoms than the formula shows
Oxygen is a gas and gases weigh more
check.why: Each oxygen atom has about sixteen times the mass of a hydrogen atom, so one oxygen outweighs two hydrogens easily.

check.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2?
check.why: The subscript 2 outside the parentheses applies to everything inside, so 3 oxygens times 2 gives 6.

lessons.title: Grams, Moles and Particles
lessons.mainIdea: Molar mass converts between grams and moles, and Avogadro's number converts between moles and particles, so any one of the three lets you find the other two.
reading: Think of the mole as a bridge with two lanes. On one side is what you can measure, mass in grams. On the other side is what you want to know, number of particles. Molar mass carries you from grams to moles. Avogadro's number carries you from moles to particles. You can cross in either direction, and every calculation in this chapter uses this bridge.

Take 9.0 grams of water. Divide by the molar mass, 18.02 grams per mole, and you get 0.50 mole. Multiply by 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd power, and you get about 3.0 times 10 to the 23rd power molecules. Going the other way is just as easy. A chemist who needs 2.0 moles of sodium chloride multiplies by 58.44 grams per mole and weighs out 117 grams. The balance does the counting.

The trick is to keep units attached to every number. Grams divided by grams-per-mole gives moles. Moles times particles-per-mole gives particles. If your units do not cancel to what you want, you multiplied when you should have divided. Chemists call this *dimensional analysis*, and it catches more mistakes than any calculator.

Why does this matter outside a classroom? A pharmacist making a solution needs a certain number of drug molecules per liter, not a certain number of grams, because the body responds to molecules. A fertilizer plant needs the right count of nitrogen atoms per bag. A jeweler testing gold wants the ratio of gold atoms to copper atoms. In every case, the path runs from a balance, through molar mass, to a count.

words.d: solving a problem by tracking units so that they cancel to the unit you want
a ratio equal to one, such as 18.02 g per 1 mol of water, used to change units
a single atom, molecule or ion, the thing a mole counts

look.title: The Jeweler's Balance
look.text: A ring is stamped 18 karat, meaning 18 parts gold and 6 parts copper by mass, or 75 percent gold. It has a mass of 8.0 grams. Gold's molar mass is about 197 g/mol and copper's is about 63.5 g/mol. A student says the ring must contain three times as many gold atoms as copper atoms because it is three-quarters gold.
look.prompt: Is the student right? Work out roughly how many moles of each metal the ring holds, and explain what the student mixed up.

check.q: How many moles are in 36 grams of water (molar mass 18 g/mol)?
check.why: Grams divided by grams per mole gives moles: 36 divided by 18 equals 2.

check.q: A student wants 0.25 mole of NaCl (58.44 g/mol). What mass should be weighed out?
check.why: Moles times molar mass gives grams: 0.25 times 58.44 is about 14.6 grams.

check.q: Which step turns a number of moles into a number of molecules?
check.why: Avogadro's number is the number of particles per mole, so multiplying moles by it gives particles.

lessons.title: Balancing Equations
lessons.mainIdea: Atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction, so a balanced equation must show the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.
reading: Strike a match and the wood burns away to almost nothing. It looks like matter vanished. In 1789 the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier showed, with sealed flasks and a very good balance, that it does not. The mass of the ash plus the gases that escaped equals the mass of the match plus the oxygen it used. Atoms rearrange. They do not disappear. This is the *law of conservation of mass*, and every chemical equation must obey it.

A chemical equation is a sentence written in formulas. Methane burning in oxygen reads CH4 + O2 gives CO2 + H2O. Count the atoms. The left has 1 carbon, 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens. The right has 1 carbon, 2 hydrogens and 3 oxygens. Hydrogen and oxygen do not match, so the equation is unbalanced. It describes something impossible.

To fix it, you may change only the numbers in front of formulas, called *coefficients*. You may never change a subscript, because that would turn one substance into a different one. H2O is water; H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a bleach. Put a 2 in front of H2O to get 4 hydrogens on the right. Now the right has 4 oxygens, so put a 2 in front of O2. The balanced equation is CH4 + 2 O2 gives CO2 + 2 H2O. One carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on each side.

A useful order is to balance metals first, then nonmetals, then hydrogen, then oxygen, saving any element that appears alone, like O2, for last, since changing its coefficient affects nothing else. Check every atom at the end. A balanced equation is more than tidy bookkeeping. Its coefficients are the recipe, the exact ratio in which molecules react, and the rest of this chapter depends on them.

words.d: in a chemical reaction the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants
the number written in front of a formula in an equation, showing how many of that unit take part
a substance that is used up in a reaction, written on the left of the arrow
a substance that is made in a reaction, written on the right of the arrow

look.title: Lavoisier on Nothing Lost
look.text: Lavoisier wrote that in every operation of art and nature, nothing is created; an equal quantity of matter exists before and after the experiment. The elements are merely rearranged, and the whole art of doing experiments in chemistry rests on this principle.
look.cite: Antoine Lavoisier, Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, 1789 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Lavoisier needed sealed containers to reach this conclusion. What would an open flask have hidden from him when a candle burned inside it?

check.q: Why can you change coefficients but not subscripts when balancing?
choices: Subscripts are too small to read
Changing a subscript changes the identity of the substance
check.why: A subscript is part of the formula. Changing H2O to H2O2 describes a different compound, not a different amount.

check.q: Which equation is balanced?
check.why: 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O has 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens on each side. The others have unequal counts.

check.q: A sealed flask holds a candle and air. The candle burns out. What happens to the flask's total mass?
choices: It decreases as wax burns away
check.why: Nothing enters or leaves a sealed flask. Atoms rearrange into new substances, but the total mass is conserved.

lessons.title: Mole Ratios
lessons.mainIdea: The coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios, and those ratios, combined with molar masses, let you predict the mass of any product from the mass of any reactant.
reading: A balanced equation is a recipe written in moles. Read 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O as: two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to make two moles of water. The numbers 2, 1 and 2 are the *mole ratio*. Double the hydrogen and you need double the oxygen and get double the water. Everything scales together. Using these ratios to predict amounts is called *stoichiometry*, from Greek words meaning to measure elements.

Here is the standard path. Start with a mass of one substance. Convert it to moles using molar mass. Use the mole ratio from the equation to find moles of the substance you want. Convert those moles back to grams. Three steps: grams to moles, moles to moles, moles to grams. Try it: how much water forms when 4.0 grams of hydrogen burns completely? 4.0 grams of H2 is 2.0 moles. The ratio of H2 to H2O is 2 to 2, so 2.0 moles of water form. That is 2.0 times 18.02, about 36 grams of water.

Notice that 4 grams of hydrogen gave 36 grams of water. The extra 32 grams came from oxygen. Mass is conserved, but the mass ratio, 4 to 32 to 36, is not the mole ratio, 2 to 1 to 2. Never take a ratio straight from the grams. You must pass through moles, because the equation counts molecules, and molecules of different substances have different masses.

Industry runs on these calculations. A steel plant knows how many tons of coke it must burn per ton of iron ore. A bakery knows how much baking soda releases the right volume of carbon dioxide for a batch of dough. The airbag engineer knows that 2 moles of sodium azide, about 130 grams, release 3 moles of nitrogen. The ratio in the equation is the whole design.

words.d: using the mole ratios in a balanced equation to calculate amounts of reactants and products
the ratio of coefficients for two substances in a balanced equation
the amount of product a reaction makes

look.title: Two Recipes, Same Ingredients
look.text: A cook's recipe says 2 eggs plus 1 cup of flour make 1 batch of pasta. A student has 12 eggs and 8 cups of flour. Chemistry's version reads 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O. Eggs and flour have different masses, just as hydrogen and oxygen molecules do, yet the recipe counts them by number, not by weight.
look.prompt: How many batches can the cook make, and which ingredient is left over? Then explain why a chemist must convert grams to moles before using a recipe like this.

check.q: In 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O, how many moles of oxygen are needed to react with 6 moles of hydrogen?
check.why: The ratio of H2 to O2 is 2 to 1, so 6 moles of H2 need 3 moles of O2.

check.q: What is the correct order of steps to find the mass of product from the mass of a reactant?
choices: Grams to grams using the coefficients directly
Grams to moles, moles to moles by ratio, moles to grams
Moles to grams, then grams to moles
Grams to particles, then particles to grams
check.why: The mole ratio applies only to moles, so you must convert into moles, apply the ratio, then convert back.

check.q: Why do 4 grams of hydrogen and 32 grams of oxygen combine in a 2 to 1 mole ratio rather than a 4 to 32 mass ratio?
choices: Because oxygen molecules are sixteen times heavier than hydrogen molecules
Because oxygen is a larger volume of gas
Because mass is not conserved in this reaction
check.why: An O2 molecule has a mass of 32 compared to 2 for H2. Equal moles of each have very different masses, so the mass ratio and mole ratio differ.

lessons.title: Limiting Reactant and Yield
lessons.mainIdea: The reactant that runs out first limits how much product can form, and the percent yield compares what a reaction actually made with that maximum.
reading: You have 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese. Each sandwich needs 2 bread and 1 cheese. You can make 3 sandwiches, not 5, and 4 slices of bread are left over. Cheese is the *limiting reactant*: it runs out first and sets the amount of product. Bread is the *excess reactant*. Chemistry works the same way. Reactants are almost never mixed in the exact ratio of the equation, so one of them always limits.

To find the limiting reactant, convert each reactant to moles, then ask how much product each could make on its own. The smaller answer wins. Suppose 4.0 grams of hydrogen (2.0 moles) meets 16 grams of oxygen (0.50 mole). Hydrogen alone could make 2.0 moles of water. Oxygen, in the ratio 1 O2 to 2 H2O, could make only 1.0 mole. Oxygen limits. Only 1.0 mole of water forms, and 1.0 mole of hydrogen sits unreacted.

The amount of product the limiting reactant allows is the *theoretical yield*, the most you could possibly get. Real reactions rarely reach it. Some product stays stuck to the glassware. Some reactant takes a side path to something else. Some reactions simply stop before finishing. The amount you actually collect is the *actual yield*, and the *percent yield* is actual divided by theoretical times 100.

Percent yield is a report card on a procedure. A drug company making a medicine in ten steps, each at 80 percent yield, ends with only about 11 percent of what it started with, because 0.8 multiplied by itself ten times is about 0.11. That is why chemists spend careers pushing each step toward 100 percent. In an airbag, an excess of azide is deliberate, so the igniter is never the limiting factor and the bag always fills.

words.d: the reactant that is used up first and so decides how much product can form
a reactant that is left over after the limiting reactant is used up
the largest amount of product possible, calculated from the limiting reactant
the amount of product really collected from a reaction
actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times 100

look.title: The Ten-Step Synthesis
look.text: A lab makes a new compound in a chain of steps. Each step uses the product of the one before as its starting material. The chemists are proud that every step reaches a 90 percent yield. The project manager asks why, after eight steps, only about 43 percent of the original material has become the final product.
look.prompt: Show how a 90 percent yield repeated eight times gives about 43 percent overall. Which single step would be most valuable to improve, and why might the answer be any of them?

check.q: Which reactant is the limiting reactant?
choices: The one with the largest mass
The one with the most moles
The one that would make the least product
The one written first in the equation
check.why: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, which is the one that could make the least product on its own.

check.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 20.0 grams. The student collects 15.0 grams. What is the percent yield?
check.why: Percent yield is actual over theoretical: 15.0 divided by 20.0 times 100 equals 75 percent.

check.q: A student reports a percent yield of 115 percent. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The product still contains water or other impurities that added mass
The limiting reactant was in excess
The theoretical yield was too high
check.why: You cannot make more than the theoretical yield. A result above 100 percent usually means the product was wet or impure.

lessons.title: Pressure, Volume and Temperature
lessons.mainIdea: For a fixed amount of gas, pressure and volume are inversely related, while volume and pressure each rise in proportion to absolute temperature.
reading: Squeeze a sealed plastic bottle and it pushes back. Leave a balloon in a hot car and it swells. Take a bag of chips onto a plane and it puffs up as the cabin pressure drops. Gases respond to squeezing and heating in ways that liquids and solids barely do, and those responses follow simple rules that were among the first quantitative laws in chemistry.

In 1662 Robert Boyle trapped air in a J-shaped glass tube with mercury and measured how the air shrank as he added more mercury. Doubling the pressure halved the volume. Tripling it cut the volume to a third. *Boyle's law* says that for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure times volume is constant. Gas at 1 atmosphere in 6 liters, squeezed to 3 atmospheres, occupies 2 liters. This is why a scuba diver's lungs, full of air at depth, would burst if the diver held that breath while rising.

Heat a gas and it expands. Jacques Charles in the 1780s and Joseph Gay-Lussac around 1802 measured how much. Volume grows in a straight line with temperature. Extend that line downward and every gas shrinks toward zero volume at the same temperature, about minus 273 degrees Celsius. That point is *absolute zero*, and a temperature scale starting there, the *kelvin* scale, makes the law simple. *Charles's law*: at constant pressure, volume divided by kelvin temperature is constant. Warm a gas from 300 K to 600 K and its volume doubles.

Hold the volume fixed instead, as in a sealed steel tank, and pressure rises in proportion to kelvin temperature. That is why aerosol cans warn against heat, and why tire pressure climbs after a long drive. Always convert to kelvins: add 273.15 to the Celsius reading. Going from 20 degrees to 40 degrees Celsius is not a doubling. It is 293 K to 313 K, a rise of about 7 percent.

words.d: force per unit area; for a gas, the push of its molecules on the walls of a container
at constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a fixed amount of gas multiply to a constant
at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is proportional to its kelvin temperature
the lowest possible temperature, 0 kelvin, about minus 273 degrees Celsius
the temperature scale that starts at absolute zero; kelvins equal degrees Celsius plus 273.15

look.title: Boyle's Law in a Syringe
look.cite: calculated from Boyle's law for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature
look.prompt: Multiply each pressure by its volume. What do you notice? Predict the volume at 8.0 atm and explain what happens to the product if the gas is warmed.

check.q: A gas occupies 4.0 L at 2.0 atm. At constant temperature, what is its volume at 4.0 atm?
check.why: Boyle's law: doubling the pressure halves the volume, so 4.0 L becomes 2.0 L.

check.q: Why must temperature be in kelvins when using Charles's law?
choices: Kelvins are smaller units so the math is easier
Celsius readings are always negative for gases
Only the kelvin scale starts at zero volume, so volume is truly proportional to it
check.why: Volume is proportional to temperature only when zero on the scale is absolute zero. Doubling a Celsius reading does not double the volume.

check.q: A sealed steel tank of gas is warmed from 300 K to 450 K. What happens to the pressure?
choices: It stays the same because the volume is fixed
check.why: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature. 450 divided by 300 is 1.5, so pressure rises by 50 percent.

lessons.title: The Ideal Gas Law
lessons.mainIdea: PV equals nRT ties pressure, volume, moles and temperature into one equation, and it lets stoichiometry predict the volume of a gas.
reading: Boyle's law, Charles's law and Avogadro's idea that equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules all describe one gas from different angles. Combine them and you get a single equation: PV = nRT. P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, T is kelvin temperature, and R is a constant that makes the units agree. This is the *ideal gas law*. With any three of the four variables, it gives you the fourth.

R, the *gas constant*, is 0.08206 liter-atmospheres per mole-kelvin when pressure is in atmospheres and volume in liters, or 8.314 joules per mole-kelvin in SI units. Plug in 1 mole at 1 atmosphere and 273 K, the conditions chemists call *standard temperature and pressure* or STP, and V comes out to 22.4 liters. Warm that mole to 25 degrees Celsius, 298 K, and it fills about 24.5 liters. Every gas, hydrogen or carbon dioxide or nitrogen, takes up the same volume per mole, because the volume depends on the number of molecules, not their size.

This is the link between the balance and the bag. Stoichiometry gives moles of gas. The ideal gas law turns moles into liters. Two moles of sodium azide, 130 grams, release 3 moles of nitrogen. At 25 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, that is 3 times 24.5, about 74 liters. Hot gas fresh from the reaction takes up even more, and it pushes harder, which is exactly what the designers want in the first milliseconds.

The law also works backwards. Weigh a flask of unknown gas, measure its volume, temperature and pressure, solve for n, and divide mass by moles to get the molar mass. That is how nineteenth-century chemists identified gases and, following Stanislao Cannizzaro's argument in 1858, finally settled the atomic masses of the elements. Avogadro's ignored idea became the key to the whole periodic table.

words.d: PV = nRT, the equation relating pressure, volume, moles and kelvin temperature of a gas
R, the number that makes the ideal gas law balance: 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.314 J/(mol·K)
STP: 0 degrees Celsius (273 K) and 1 atmosphere, at which one mole of gas fills 22.4 L
the volume of one mole of gas, about 22.4 L at STP and about 24.5 L at 25 degrees Celsius

look.title: A Balloon in a Freezer
look.text: A student fills a balloon with 0.10 mole of helium in a kitchen at 22 degrees Celsius, then puts it in a freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius. Overnight it shrinks noticeably but does not deflate. Air pressure in the kitchen and the freezer is the same, about 1 atmosphere.
look.prompt: Convert both temperatures to kelvins and use PV = nRT to predict the balloon's volume before and after. Why does the balloon not shrink by half even though the Celsius reading fell so far?

check.q: What volume does 1 mole of any ideal gas occupy at STP?
check.why: At 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere, PV = nRT gives 22.4 liters for one mole of any gas.

check.q: Why does 1 mole of hydrogen fill the same volume as 1 mole of carbon dioxide at the same T and P?
choices: Because the two gases have the same molar mass
Because the volume of a gas depends on the number of molecules, not their size
Because hydrogen molecules expand to match carbon dioxide
Because both gases are made of the same atoms
check.why: Gas molecules are far apart, so the space each takes is set by motion and collisions, not by the size of the molecule itself.

check.q: Which measurement is NOT needed to find the molar mass of an unknown gas with PV = nRT?
check.why: Mass, volume, pressure and temperature let you solve for moles and then mass per mole. Color plays no part.

lessons.title: Molecules in Motion
lessons.mainIdea: Gas laws follow from a model of tiny, fast, constantly colliding molecules, and real gases stray from that model only when pushed close together or cooled toward liquefying.
reading: Why does a gas obey such simple laws? The answer is the *kinetic-molecular theory*, built up in the 1800s. Its picture has a few parts. A gas is mostly empty space, with molecules far apart compared to their size. The molecules move in straight lines until they collide, with each other or the walls, and the collisions lose no energy. And the average kinetic energy of the molecules depends only on the kelvin temperature. Higher temperature means faster molecules.

Pressure, in this picture, is molecules hitting the walls. Squeeze the volume in half and each molecule reaches a wall twice as often, so pressure doubles. That is Boyle's law. Heat the gas and the molecules hit harder and more often, so pressure rises. That is Gay-Lussac's law. Because equal numbers of molecules at the same temperature deliver the same average kick, equal volumes at the same T and P hold equal numbers. That is Avogadro's law. One model explains all of them.

The numbers are startling. At room temperature, nitrogen molecules move at roughly 500 meters per second on average, faster than sound. Lighter molecules move faster: hydrogen at about 1,900 meters per second. Yet a bottle of perfume opened across a room takes minutes to smell, because each molecule collides billions of times per second and staggers rather than flies. The molecules do not all share one speed. Some crawl, some race, and the spread widens as the gas warms.

Real molecules are not points, and they do attract one another slightly. At ordinary pressures this hardly matters, and the ideal gas law works to within a percent or so. Crush a gas to hundreds of atmospheres, or cool it toward its boiling point, and the molecules' own volume and their mutual attraction start to show. Pressure comes out lower than predicted, then the gas condenses. Johannes van der Waals added two correction terms in 1873 to handle exactly this, and his equation still guides the design of tanks that hold liquefied gases.

words.d: the model of a gas as tiny, widely spaced molecules in constant, random, elastic motion
the energy of motion; for gas molecules its average is set by the kelvin temperature
a collision in which no kinetic energy is lost
an actual gas, whose molecules have volume and attract each other, unlike an ideal gas
the spreading of one substance through another by random molecular motion

look.title: Typical Molecular Speeds at 25 °C
look.prompt: What pattern links molar mass to speed? Why do the lightest gases, hydrogen and helium, slowly leak out of Earth's atmosphere while nitrogen and oxygen stay?

check.q: According to kinetic-molecular theory, what is gas pressure?
choices: The weight of the gas pressing down
Molecules colliding with the walls of the container
The heat stored in the gas
check.why: Pressure is the force of countless molecular collisions on each unit of wall area.

check.q: Which molecules move fastest on average at a given temperature?
choices: The ones with the greatest mass
The ones with the least mass
All molecules move at the same speed
The ones with the most atoms
check.why: At one temperature all gases share the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules must move faster.

check.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave least like an ideal gas?
check.why: At high pressure the molecules' own volume matters, and at low temperature their attractions matter. Both push the gas away from ideal behavior.

lessons.title: Sizing the Airbag
lessons.mainIdea: An airbag's charge is designed by working backward from the bag's volume through the ideal gas law and the mole ratio to a mass of solid.
reading: Now put every tool together on one problem. A driver-side airbag must fill a bag of about 60 liters with nitrogen. Suppose the gas in the bag ends up near 1 atmosphere and, for a first estimate, near room temperature, 298 K. How much sodium azide is needed? Start with the ideal gas law. n = PV divided by RT = 1 times 60 divided by 0.08206 times 298, about 2.5 moles of nitrogen.

Next, the mole ratio. The decomposition is 2 NaN3 gives 2 Na + 3 N2, so 2 moles of azide give 3 moles of nitrogen. To get 2.5 moles of N2 you need 2.5 times 2 divided by 3, about 1.6 moles of NaN3. Finally, molar mass. Sodium azide is 22.99 plus 3 times 14.01, about 65.0 grams per mole. So 1.6 moles is about 105 grams. Real modules use less, because the gas is very hot when the bag fills and hot gas takes more space per mole. The estimate lands in the right range, which is what a first calculation is for.

The design has to handle more than the ideal case. The bag must vent so the driver's head meets a cushion that is already deflating, not a hard wall of gas. The temperature of the gas must stay safe. The solid must not decompose on its own in a car parked in the Arizona sun. And the leftover sodium must be turned into something harmless, which is why the potassium nitrate and silica are there. Each of those is another stoichiometry problem.

Since the early 2000s most manufacturers have moved to other propellants that produce less toxic residue and are safer to handle in factories and scrapyards. The chemistry changed; the calculation did not. Whatever the solid, the engineer measures the bag, converts liters to moles with PV = nRT, walks the mole ratio back to the reactant, and converts to grams. That chain of reasoning is the whole chapter in one problem.

words.d: a reaction in which one compound breaks into two or more simpler substances
a substance that produces a large volume of gas quickly to push or inflate something
the solid material left behind after a reaction

look.title: The Passenger Bag
look.text: A passenger-side airbag is larger than the driver's because the passenger sits farther from the dashboard. Suppose it holds about 130 liters. An engineer proposes simply doubling the driver-side charge of sodium azide. A colleague objects that the passenger bag's gas will reach the same temperature and pressure as the driver's, so the answer should come from the equation, not from a rule of thumb.
look.prompt: Using 24.5 L per mole and the 2 to 3 ratio of NaN3 to N2, estimate the mass of azide for a 130 L bag. Is doubling a 60 L charge close enough? Why might an engineer add a safety margin?

check.q: What is the first step in sizing an airbag charge from the bag's volume?
choices: Balance the equation for sodium reacting with water
Convert liters of gas to moles with the ideal gas law
Measure the speed of the crash
check.why: The bag's volume is known. PV = nRT turns that volume into the moles of nitrogen the bag needs.

check.q: Why do real modules use less azide than the room-temperature estimate suggests?
choices: Sodium azide has a smaller molar mass in practice
The gas is hot when it fills the bag, so each mole takes up more space
The reaction makes 5 moles of nitrogen instead of 3
The bag is smaller than 60 liters
check.why: Hot gas expands. By Charles's law each mole of nitrogen fills more volume, so fewer moles, and less solid, are needed.

check.q: Which ratio is used to go from moles of nitrogen to moles of sodium azide?
choices: 3 N2 for every 2 NaN3, from the balanced equation
check.why: The coefficients of 2 NaN3 gives 2 Na + 3 N2 set the ratio. Molar masses convert grams, not moles.

lessons.title: Fast Reactions and Safety
lessons.mainIdea: How fast a reaction runs depends on temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts, and the same chemistry that saves lives in a crash demands care in the lab.
reading: Stoichiometry tells you how much. It says nothing about how fast. A log in a fireplace and a cloud of sawdust in a grain elevator hold the same chemistry, wood plus oxygen, yet one burns for an hour and the other can explode. Speed is a separate question, answered by *reaction rate*: how much reactant is used up, or product made, per second.

Molecules react when they collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Anything that makes collisions more frequent or more energetic speeds a reaction. Raise the temperature, and molecules move faster and hit harder. Raise the concentration, or the pressure of a gas, and collisions come more often. Grind a solid into powder, and far more of its surface is exposed. That last one is why the sodium azide in an airbag is a fine powder, why grain dust explodes, and why a sugar cube resists a flame that ignites powdered sugar instantly.

The energy a collision needs is the *activation energy*, a hill the reactants must climb before they can roll down to products. Sodium azide sits stable for years because room temperature almost never gives a collision that energy. The igniter supplies it, and once the first bit decomposes, the heat it releases carries the rest over the hill in a few milliseconds. A *catalyst* offers a lower hill and speeds a reaction without being used up. Your body runs on thousands of them, the enzymes.

In the lab, the rules of rate are the rules of safety. Keep reactive powders in small amounts and away from heat. Add a concentrated acid to water, never water to acid, because the heat released near the surface can flash the water to steam and spray acid. Use a fume hood for anything that gives off gas, since a mole of gas is 24 liters. Wear goggles every time. A chemist who can calculate how much gas a reaction makes, and how quickly, is a chemist who does not get surprised.

words.d: how quickly a reaction happens, measured as change in amount of reactant or product per unit time
the minimum energy colliding molecules need for a reaction to occur
a substance that speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy and is not used up
the amount of a solid's surface exposed to other reactants; powders have far more than lumps

look.title: Boyle's Spring of the Air, 1662
look.text: Boyle described air as behaving like a spring: when compressed it pushes back, and the more it is squeezed the harder it pushes. He reported measurements showing that when the pressure on a trapped volume of air was doubled, the volume was reduced to about half.
look.cite: Robert Boyle, New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air, 1662 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Boyle imagined air as a spring. Using kinetic-molecular theory, explain what is actually pushing back when a gas is compressed.

check.q: Why does powdered sugar ignite more easily than a sugar cube?
choices: Powdered sugar has a different chemical formula
The powder has far more surface area exposed to oxygen
The cube contains water that puts out the flame
Powder is warmer than a cube
check.why: Reactions happen at surfaces. Grinding a solid exposes vastly more surface, so far more collisions with oxygen occur each second.

check.q: What does a catalyst do?
choices: Increases the amount of product beyond the theoretical yield
Lowers the activation energy without being used up
Raises the temperature of the reaction
check.why: A catalyst offers an easier path, a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It is unchanged at the end.

check.q: Why is sodium azide stable in a parked car for years but decomposes in milliseconds in a crash?
choices: Room temperature rarely supplies the activation energy; the igniter does
Sodium azide only reacts when it is wet
The crash changes the molar mass of the azide
Cars are sealed so no oxygen reaches the powder
check.why: The reaction needs a high activation energy. Ordinary heat almost never provides it, but the igniter's heat starts a self-sustaining decomposition.

review.q: One mole of any substance always contains the same what?
review.why: A mole is a count, 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd power particles, regardless of the substance.

review.q: What is the approximate molar mass of sodium azide, NaN3 (Na 22.99, N 14.01)?
In 2 NaN3 gives 2 Na + 3 N2, how many moles of nitrogen come from 4 moles of sodium azide?
review.why: The ratio is 2 NaN3 to 3 N2. Four moles of azide is twice that, so 6 moles of nitrogen.

review.q: Which statement about a limiting reactant is correct?
choices: It is completely used up and controls how much product forms
It is always the reactant with the smaller mass
It is left over when the reaction ends
It is the reactant with the largest coefficient
review.why: The limiting reactant runs out first. Its amount, through the mole ratio, sets the theoretical yield.

review.q: A gas at 300 K and 2.0 atm is heated to 600 K in a rigid container. What is the new pressure?
review.why: At constant volume pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature. Doubling T doubles P to 4.0 atm.

review.q: How many liters does 2.0 moles of an ideal gas occupy at STP?
review.why: One mole occupies 22.4 L at STP, so two moles occupy 44.8 L.

review.q: Which change would slow a reaction between a solid and a gas?
review.why: Cooling reduces molecular speed and energy, so fewer collisions have enough energy to react.

review.q: A student measures 12 grams of a gas that fills 22.4 L at STP. What is its molar mass?
review.why: 22.4 L at STP is 1 mole. Twelve grams per mole gives a molar mass of 12 g/mol.
